entries.definition: The marks over French letters. They change pronunciation and sometimes meaning, and they are expected in written work.
entries.example: *é* as in *fatigué*, *è* as in *inquiète*, *ç* as in *ça*. **Ou** means *or*; **où** means *where* — the accent is the whole difference.

entries.definition: An adjective changes to match the gender and number of what it describes. Usually **-e** for feminine and **-s** for plural, and it often sounds identical, so it is purely a written mark.
entries.example: A boy writes *je suis fatigué*; a girl writes *je suis fatiguée*. *Inquiet* becomes *inquiète*.

entries.definition: With **être**, the past participle agrees with the subject. With a **reflexive** verb it agrees with the reflexive pronoun — but only when that pronoun is the **direct object**. If a noun follows the participle, that noun is the direct object instead, and there is no agreement.
entries.example: *Elle s'est blessé**e*** agrees, because *se* is the object. *Elle s'est blessé la main* does **not**, because *la main* is. Test: is there a noun straight after the participle?

entries.definition: The word before a noun. **Definite**: le, la, l', les (*the*). **Indefinite**: un, une, des (*a*, *some*). **Partitive**: du, de la, de l', des, for an unspecified amount.
entries.example: *J'écoute **de la** musique* — *I listen to music*. After a quantity word the article collapses to plain **de**: *beaucoup **de** devoirs*.

entries.definition: The verb that carries the tense in a compound tense. In the perfect it is **avoir** for most verbs, **être** for reflexive verbs and a group of movement verbs.
entries.example: *J'**ai** mangé* uses avoir. *Je **suis** tombé* and *je me **suis** couché* use être. Using avoir with a reflexive verb is always wrong.

entries.definition: *To need to*. The **de** is compulsory before the infinitive, and dropping it costs a mark.
entries.example: *J'ai besoin de dormir* — *I need to sleep*. Never *j'ai besoin dormir*.

entries.definition: *To have a pain in*, used for every ache. The **à** contracts with the article in front of the body part, so you have to know the part's gender.
entries.example: *J'ai mal **au** dos* (le dos), *j'ai mal **à la** tête* (la tête), *j'ai mal **aux** dents* (les dents). *À le* and *à les* are never written.

entries.definition: A word that looks like its English equivalent, so it can be read without knowing it. French is full of them, which makes reading papers more approachable than they look.
entries.example: *le stress*, *la musique*, *essentiel*, *le sport*, *la famille*. Guessing from a cognate is a legitimate reading-paper strategy.

entries.definition: A word that joins clauses and lifts a one-clause sentence into something that scores: *et*, *mais*, *parce que*, *car*, *donc*, *puisque*, *par contre*, *cependant*.
entries.example: *Je fais du sport **parce que** ça me détend.* Using **car** as well as *parce que* shows range, and both mean *because*.

entries.definition: *For* or *since*, with a situation that is **still going on**. French keeps the **present** tense where English switches to a past.
entries.example: *J'ai mal à la gorge **depuis** deux jours* — *I **have had** a sore throat for two days*, not *I have*. The mismatch is a favourite of the reading paper.

entries.definition: Turning a bare clause into one that earns marks: add a time phrase, a reason and an opinion. Each addition is separately credited.
entries.example: *Je fais du sport.* → *Normalement, je fais du sport parce que ça me détend, et à mon avis c'est essentiel.* Same vocabulary, several times the credit.

entries.definition: A word that looks like an English one but means something else. The reading paper sets them deliberately.
entries.example: *Sensible* means *sensitive*, not sensible. *Actuellement* means *currently*, not actually. *Rester* means *to stay*, not to rest.

entries.definition: The part the future endings attach to. Regular verbs use the infinitive; a small group of very common verbs have their own stem, which must be learnt.
entries.example: *être* → **ser-**, *avoir* → **aur-**, *aller* → **ir-**, *faire* → **fer-**, *pouvoir* → **pourr-**, *venir* → **viendr-**, *voir* → **verr-**. Every one still ends in *-r*.

entries.definition: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, which decides the article and any adjective. Learn each noun **with** its article.
entries.example: *Le sommeil* is masculine, *la santé* is feminine. Learning *santé* alone leaves you guessing later.

entries.definition: *You must* or *it is necessary to*, always followed by an infinitive. It never changes its form, whoever you are talking about. The negative is **il ne faut pas**, *you must not*.
entries.example: *Il faut dormir huit heures par nuit.* *Il ne faut pas travailler tout le temps.*

entries.definition: The past tense for description, background and repeated actions: *was doing*, *used to do*. Endings *-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient* on the *nous* stem.
entries.example: *Je **faisais** du vélo quand je **suis tombé*** — imperfect for the background, perfect for the event. *J'**étais** malade*, *j'**avais** de la fièvre*.

entries.definition: The unchanged form of a verb, as it appears in a dictionary: *parler*, *finir*, *vendre*, *se détendre*. It follows **pour**, **il faut**, **je voudrais** and **avoir besoin de**.
entries.example: *Il faut **dormir*** — *you must sleep*. The verb after *il faut* never changes.

entries.definition: *Aller* in the present plus an infinitive: what you are going to do. Simpler than the simple future and worth having ready.
entries.example: *Je vais me reposer* — *I am going to rest*. *Nous allons faire du sport.*

entries.definition: **Ne … pas** wraps around the verb. With a reflexive verb it wraps around the pronoun **and** the verb, so the **ne** comes first of all.
entries.example: *Je ne me sens pas bien* — *I don't feel well*. Not *je me ne sens pas bien*.

entries.definition: A set phrase for introducing what you think. Vary them: repeating *je pense que* is marked as a narrow range.
entries.example: *À mon avis*, *selon moi*, *je trouve que*, *d'après moi*, *je pense que*. *À mon avis, le sommeil est essentiel.*

entries.definition: The part of a compound tense that carries the meaning. Formed from the infinitive: *-er* → **-é**, *-ir* → **-i**, *-re* → **-u**, with a set of irregulars to learn.
entries.example: *tomber* → **tombé**, *finir* → **fini**, *vendre* → **vendu**. Irregular: *faire* → **fait**, *avoir* → **eu**, *être* → **été**, *prendre* → **pris**.

entries.definition: The tense for a completed past action: an auxiliary (**avoir** or **être**) in the present plus a past participle. **All reflexive verbs take être**, as do a small group of movement verbs, and with être the participle agrees with the subject.
entries.example: *J'ai mangé* — *I ate*. *Je me suis couché* — *I went to bed*; a girl writes *je me suis couchée*.

entries.definition: *In order to*. When you are talking about yourself, a reflexive verb after **pour** keeps **your** pronoun.
entries.example: *Pour me détendre, j'écoute de la musique* — *to relax, I listen to music*. Writing *pour se détendre* about yourself is wrong.

entries.definition: The tense for what happens now or regularly. Endings depend on whether the infinitive ends *-er*, *-ir* or *-re*.
entries.example: *-er*: je parl**e**, tu parl**es**, il parl**e**, nous parl**ons**, vous parl**ez**, ils parl**ent**. *Je me détends* is an *-re* verb: the *je* ending is **-s**.

entries.definition: After **quand**, **dès que** and **lorsque**, French uses the **future** where English uses a present. This is the one place the two languages genuinely disagree, and it is examined directly.
entries.example: *Quand j'**aurai** dix-huit ans, je voyagerai* — *when I **am** eighteen, I will travel*. Contrast **si**, which takes the present.

entries.definition: **Beaucoup de**, **plus de**, **trop de**, **assez de** and **peu de** always take plain **de**, never *du* or *des*, whatever follows.
entries.example: *J'ai beaucoup **de** devoirs*, not *beaucoup des devoirs*. *Je voudrais faire plus **de** sport*.

entries.definition: The little word before a reflexive verb that matches the subject: je **me**, tu **te**, il/elle/on **se**, nous **nous**, vous **vous**, ils/elles **se**.
entries.example: *Nous nous sentons bien* — both words are *nous*, the subject and the pronoun. Dropping it (*je couche*) is the commonest error in this unit.

entries.definition: A verb whose action points back at the subject, carrying a pronoun before it: **me, te, se, nous, vous, se**. English usually drops the pronoun in translation.
entries.example: *Je me couche à dix heures* — *I go to bed at ten*, not *I put myself to bed*. Before a vowel it shortens: *je m'habille*.

entries.definition: A condition with **si**, *if*. **Si never takes the future.** The pattern is *si* + **present**, then the **future** in the other half — the same as English.
entries.example: *Si je mange mieux, je **serai** en forme.* Never *si je mangerai*. The halves can swap: *J'irai à la piscine si j'ai le temps.*

entries.definition: The future in one word: a **stem** plus an ending. The endings never change — **-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont** — and are *avoir* in the present with the *av-* removed. For regular *-er* and *-ir* verbs the stem is the whole infinitive (a spelling change in the present is kept: *acheter* → *j'achèterai*); *-re* verbs drop the final **-e**.
entries.example: *parler* → *je parler**ai***; *prendre* → *je prendr**ai***. **Every future stem ends in -r**: if yours does not, it is wrong.

entries.definition: The fastest way to show range. Signal each tense with a time marker so the examiner cannot miss it.
entries.example: *Avant je **mangeais** mal* (imperfect), *mais j'**ai arrêté** le coca* (perfect), *et à l'avenir je **mangerai** mieux* (simple future). Three tenses, three time markers, one paragraph.

entries.definition: Comparing two things with **plus** … **que** (more … than), **moins** … **que** (less … than) or **aussi** … **que** (as … as). The adjective in the middle still agrees. With a noun it is **plus de** / **moins de**, with plain *de*.
entries.example: *Les légumes sont plus **sains** que les frites* — masculine plural, so *sains*. *L'eau est plus **saine** que le coca.* *Je mange plus **de** fruits.*

entries.definition: *The most* or *the least*: **le / la / les plus** (or **moins**) + adjective. When the adjective comes after the noun, the article appears twice.
entries.example: *La boisson **la plus** saine* — the healthiest drink. *Le sport **le plus** utile.* The superlative of *bon* is *le meilleur*: *la **meilleure** décision*.

entries.definition: Both mean *better*. **Meilleur** is an adjective: it goes with a **noun** and agrees. **Mieux** is an adverb: it goes with a **verb** and never changes. *Plus bon* and *plus bien* do not exist.
entries.example: *Une **meilleure** solution* — better describes a thing. *Je dors **mieux*** — better describes how you sleep. Ask *better what?*: a thing is *meilleur*, a way of doing is *mieux*.

entries.term: Verbs followed by à or de
entries.definition: Many verbs that lead into an infinitive bring **à** or **de**, which must be learnt with the verb. Others — *aimer*, *vouloir*, *pouvoir*, *devoir*, *aller* — take the infinitive directly.
entries.example: *J'essaie **d'**arrêter **de** grignoter* — each verb keeps its own *de*, and the first shortens before the vowel. *Je commence **à** faire du sport.* But *je veux manger*, with nothing.

entries.definition: *It is better to*, followed by an infinitive. Like *il faut*, it never changes its form.
entries.example: *Il vaut mieux boire de l'eau que du coca.* — It is better to drink water than cola.

entries.definition: Phrases that signal which tense a sentence needs: *quand j'étais petit* and *autrefois* for the imperfect; *d'habitude* and *chaque été* for the present; *l'année prochaine* and *à l'avenir* for the simple future; *l'année dernière* for the perfect.
entries.example: *Autrefois j'allais en Bretagne; maintenant je vais en Espagne; l'année prochaine j'irai en Italie.*

entries.definition: Two past tenses with different jobs. The **perfect** is for a single completed event (*l'année dernière je suis allé en Italie*); the **imperfect** is for a habit or for background description (*j'allais tous les ans*, *il faisait beau*, *l'hôtel était génial*).
entries.example: *Il pleuvait quand nous sommes partis.* Background in the imperfect, the event in the perfect.

entries.definition: *To* a feminine country is **en** (*en France*), a masculine one **au** (*au Portugal*), a plural one **aux** (*aux États-Unis*), a city **à** (*à Paris*). *From* is **de / du / des / de**.
entries.example: *Je vais en Espagne et je reviens d'Espagne; je vais au Maroc et je reviens du Maroc.*

entries.definition: The pronoun meaning *there*, replacing a place already mentioned. It goes immediately before the verb, and *je* becomes *j'y*.
entries.example: *Nous allons en Espagne chaque été; nous y allons en avion.* — we go there by plane.

entries.definition: *There is no / there are no*. After a negative, *un*, *une* and *du* all become **de**.
entries.example: *Il y a une piscine, mais il n'y a pas de climatisation.*

entries.definition: Both translate *to spend*, but **passer** is for time and **dépenser** is for money.
entries.example: *Nous passons deux semaines en Grèce* (we spend two weeks); *je dépense trop d'argent* (I spend too much money).

entries.definition: Transport you sit inside takes **en**: *en avion, en train, en voiture, en car, en bateau*. Transport you sit on takes **à**: *à vélo, à pied* (on foot).
entries.example: *Nous y allons en car* — by coach, not by car (*en voiture*).

entries.definition: The tense for *would*: the future stem plus the imperfect endings *-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*. Irregular stems are the future ones: *ir-, ser-, aur-, fer-, pourr-, voudr-, verr-*.
entries.example: *J'irais aux Maldives; ce serait parfait; il y aurait une piscine.* One letter from the future: *j'irai* (will) against *j'irais* (would).

entries.definition: The pattern for a dream or hypothesis: *si* followed by the imperfect, then the conditional. For a real plan it is *si* + present, then the future. Never a future or a conditional straight after *si*.
entries.example: *Si j'étais riche, j'irais au Japon* (dream); *si j'ai de l'argent, j'irai en Italie* (plan).

entries.definition: *I would like*: the polite conditional of *vouloir* and of *aimer*, followed directly by an infinitive. *Je voudrais* also opens transactional role plays.
entries.example: *J'aimerais visiter le Japon; je voudrais réserver une chambre.*

entries.definition: English *would* has two meanings. For a wish it is the conditional (*j'irais*); for a past habit, *we would go every summer*, French uses the imperfect (*nous allions*).
entries.example: *Quand j'étais petit, nous allions à la plage tous les jours* — when I was little, we would go to the beach every day.

entries.definition: Sports and outdoor activities take **faire de** with the article (*faire du vélo, de la voile, des randonnées*); games take **jouer à** (*jouer au foot, aux cartes*). *Jouer de* is only for instruments.
entries.example: *Nous avons fait de la planche à voile et nous avons joué au volley.*

entries.definition: A reflexive verb takes **être** in the perfect, with its pronoun before the auxiliary, and the participle agrees with the subject when the pronoun is the direct object.
entries.example: *Je me suis baignée dans la mer* (a girl); *nous nous sommes promenés le soir*.

entries.definition: Words that put events in order: *d'abord* (first), *ensuite* and *puis* (then), *après* (afterwards), *enfin* (finally). *Un jour* and *un soir* pick out a single event.
entries.example: *D'abord, nous avons visité Rome, puis nous sommes allés à la plage. Enfin, un soir, on a mangé des glaces.*

entries.definition: Weather is background, so it takes the imperfect: *il faisait beau*, *il faisait chaud*, *il pleuvait*, *il y avait du vent*. The events in front of it are in the perfect.
entries.example: *Il faisait chaud, alors nous sommes allés à la plage.*

entries.definition: A word that strengthens an opinion: *vraiment* (really), *tellement* (so), *assez* (quite), *trop* (too). *Tellement… que* means *so… that*.
entries.example: *C'était vraiment génial; c'était tellement ennuyeux que nous sommes rentrés tôt.*
